micromouse 4wd · aero study

Air is not what is slowing your mouse down

At 5 m/s the whole robot pushes 28.7 mN of air — about 1.33 % of its own weight, and less than the friction of its own tyres rolling. Below 2 m/s it is close to unmeasurable. This page computes that from the real CAD silhouette rather than a guess, and shows what the flow actually does in straights and in corners.

Drag versus speed

Drag grows with the square of speed, so it is negligible at 1 m/s (1.15 mN) and still small at 5 m/s. The band is the honest uncertainty in Cd for a bluff, open-wheeled, ground-proximity body (0.70–1.15); the line is Cd 0.90. The dashed line is rolling resistance — drag only catches it at 5.31 m/s.

aero drag (band = Cd 0.70–1.15) rolling resistance (Crr 0.015)

Where it sits in the force budget

The comparison that settles it: at full speed, drag is roughly a hundredth of the grip the tyres can deliver. Nothing about the robot's lap time is decided by air.

Straights and corners

In a corner the body runs at a slip angle, so it presents a slightly bigger area and picks up a side force. The slip angles here are not assumed — they are measured in sim_twin, the same offline twin that tunes the controller: 2.3° mean in corners at 0.8 m/s, 6.7° at the 95th percentile at 3 m/s. That attitude adds only 8.5 % to the frontal area, and the side force at 5 m/s is 5.23 mN — three orders of magnitude below the cornering force the tyres are already carrying.

5 m/s through a corner is not physically reachable on this robot: a 90 mm turn radius on race-glue tyres caps corner speed near 1.19 m/s on grip alone. The cornering column is the drag the robot would see at that attitude, listed at the same speeds so the comparison is like-for-like.

The wake in motion

The wake behind a bluff body is not steady — it sheds. These are the same lattice-Boltzmann solves run in time, after the start-up transient has washed out. Switch between straight and cornering attitude, and between speed and vorticity (vorticity shows the individual vortices rolling off the corners; speed shows how far the slow wake reaches).

Flow runs left to right. The body is drawn in ink; behind it the wake alternates as vortices peel off each side. In the cornering frame the shedding is asymmetric — one side separates earlier — which is the side force in the table above, and the reason a real crosswind would be felt as a small steering bias rather than as drag.

What the flow does

A 2D lattice-Boltzmann solve over the robot's real silhouette. Read these for the shape of the wake, not for a number: the lattice runs near Re 10³ while the robot at 5 m/s is at Re 39,578, so the separation points are indicative and the turbulent detail is not resolved. Every force on this page comes from the drag equation, never from these fields.

Would a wing or a diffuser help?

No — and the reason is worth understanding, because it also rules out several other intuitive fixes. Downforce scales with v², exactly like drag. But grip only matters in corners, and this robot corners at about 1.19 m/s. At that speed a realistic printed wing-and-splitter package (CL 0.3 on plan area) makes 3.3 mN of downforce — 0.2 % of the robot's weight. The aero device is asleep precisely where you need it. The assumption-free version of the same point: at 1.19 m/s the dynamic pressure is 0.85 Pa, so matching the robot's own weight would need CL ≈ 196. The best wings ever built reach 2–3.

That first estimate used a literature CL, which is an assumption, not a test — so I built the parts and measured them. A rear wing (26 mm chord at −12° on struts) and an upswept underbody diffuser were added to the robot's real side profile and the force on the body was integrated by momentum exchange across the bounce-back links:

ConfigurationMeasured CLΔCL vs bareDownforce gained at 1.19 m/sDrag penalty
baseline0.867———
rear wing0.691+0.176+1.94 mN (+0.09%)+8.8%
diffuser0.885-0.019-0.20 mN (-0.01%)-0.6%
wing + diffuser0.661+0.205+2.27 mN (+0.11%)+8.5%

The bare robot makes a little lift — the wheels are its highest surfaces, so flow accelerates over them and pulls up. The wing claws back about a quarter of that, worth 1.9 mN at corner speed, for 8.8 % more drag. The diffuser measures as doing nothing at all: at a 5 mm ride height and this Reynolds number the underbody gap is thick with boundary layer, so there is no fast, clean flow for a diffuser to expand. This is measured, and it is worse than the CL 0.3 I assumed before — and 2D simulation flatters wings, because it has no tip vortices.

Two of those bars are the whole lesson. Ballast does nothing: cornering speed is √(μgR), independent of mass — extra weight buys grip and inertia in equal measure. A passive wing does almost nothing here, not because the aerodynamics are wrong but because 1.19 m/s is too slow to load it. Even a perfect F1-grade underbody, which a 5 mm ride height over a jointed maze floor cannot physically sustain, would buy under 1 %.

What does work is force that doesn't come with mass and doesn't need speed: a suction fan pulling a partial vacuum under a skirted underbody. 250 Pa across the 12900 mm² plan area is 3.23 N — more than the robot's own weight, available at a standstill, and worth 58 % on corner speed. That is why serious mice fit fans and not wings. There is room for it: the board has a clear 32 × 32 mm window at its centre, big enough for a 28 mm fan duct, though using it means a hole through the PCB, a flexible skirt at 1–2 mm ride height, and a second battery budget.

Cheapest real gain, though, needs no hardware at all: better tyre rubber and a planner that dares to use more of the friction circle. The last bar is the same robot on tape, which is the change you already have in the simulator.

Frontal, side and plan areas rasterised at 0.5 mm from the tessellated assembly (Gear/aero_study.py); slip angles logged from sim_twin.py; flow fields from a D2Q9 lattice-Boltzmann solver over the same silhouettes (Gear/aero_flow.py). Air at 20 °C (ρ 1.204 kg/m³, ν 1.516×10⁻⁵ m²/s), robot mass 0.22 kg. Cd band and Crr are literature values for bluff ground vehicles, not measurements — they are the least certain inputs here, and the conclusion holds across the whole band.
